useful_material: This study investigated gut microbiome and metabolome associations with long-term ICI outcomes and immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in a prospective cohort of lung cancer patients (metagenome n=54, metabolome n=49). The authors grouped patients into benefit, severe irAE, and resistance categories. The severe irAE group (n=13 in metagenome cohort) included various irAE types such as cardiovascular toxicity (2 cases), muscle toxicity (1 case), endocrine, skin, and gastrointestinal toxicities, rather than focusing exclusively on colitis. Mechanistically, the authors reported that microbiota sequences from irAE patients aligned with autoimmune antigenic epitopes (molecular mimicry), particularly noting SLE-related epitopes enriched in colitis patients, and that beneficial outcomes correlated with higher short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate and propionate. Strain-level variations in Escherichia coli and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were also associated with clinical phenotypes. The authors explicitly stated in the limitations that the sample size was relatively small due to strict quality control and long-term follow-up requirements.

This study provides preclinical mechanistic evidence linking gut microbiota to PD-1 inhibitor-associated myocarditis, a non-colitis irAE. The authors established a melanoma mouse model (n=6 per group) showing that PD-1 inhibition induced myocarditis, reduced cardiac regulatory T cells (Tregs), and altered gut microbiota composition. Specific taxa (e.g., Ruminococcaceae, Flexispira) were correlated with cardiac injury markers (CK-MB, cTn-I) and Treg-related gene expression (FOXP3, IL-10). Fecal microbiota removal (antibiotic treatment) attenuated myocarditis and restored Treg levels without compromising antitumor efficacy in this model. These findings support the biological plausibility of a microbiome-immune axis in non-colitis irAEs.
